# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
# Review of the Varden County 30-Hour Week Trial

This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot, and it fixes most of that paper's problems:
- a randomised control group;
- administrative output measures instead of manager ratings;
- actual hours from timesheets;
- stratification by type of work before randomisation;
- a registered plan, with exploratory work clearly labelled.

The headline findings are mostly appropriately hedged. The main remaining issues are the small-cluster inference, a few outcomes reported outside the registered framework, possible spillovers between offices, the interpretation of the counter-office per-hour gain, and the absence of cost.

## Arithmetic checks

The numbers are internally consistent:
- **Hours.** 37.9 → 33.0 is −12.9%, and 37.6 → 31.2 is −17.0%. Scheduled hours fall from 37.5 to 30, which is −20%.
- **Output per actual hour, case-processing.** 0.979 / 0.87 = 1.125, so +12.5%.
- **Output per actual hour, counter.** 0.886 / 0.83 = 1.067, so +6.7%.
- **Against scheduled hours.** 0.979 / 0.80 = 1.224, matching the stated "22%".
- **Confidence intervals.** The per-hour CIs are roughly what you get by dividing the output-per-FTE CIs by the hours ratio. For example, (−6.8, +2.6) / 0.87 gives about (+7.1, +17.9), against the reported (+6.9, +18.4). That is consistent once uncertainty in hours is added.

## 1. Inference with few clusters

There are 24 clusters in total, but each stratum is analysed separately: 14 offices in case-processing and **only 10 (5 v 5) in the counter stratum**. Conventional cluster-robust standard errors are unreliable with this few clusters and tend to be too small.

This matters most for the counter per-hour gain, whose lower bound is +0.4%. I'd ask the authors to:
- report wild-cluster bootstrap or randomisation-inference p-values; and
- state what the registered protocol specified for small-cluster inference.

## 2. Several outcomes are reported outside the difference-in-differences framework

The registered analysis is difference-in-differences against control. Several outcomes are not reported that way:

- **Waiting time** (4.2 → 6.9 minutes) is a treated-only before/after comparison with no control trend. It is also a registered secondary outcome, so it should have a DiD estimate with a CI.
- **Abandoned calls** (6% → 10%) are treated-only and don't appear among the registered outcomes.
- **Quality** ("3.1% v 3.0%", "11.8% v 10.9%") gives levels with no CI. It isn't clear which figure is treated, or whether these are differences-in-differences.
- **Resignations** (3.9% v 7.4%) are a raw comparison of levels.
- **Sick days** (−29%) are pooled across strata with no CI, although other outcomes are reported by stratum.

The directions are plausible. But the paper's main strength is its registered design, and these figures borrow its credibility without meeting its standard.

## 3. Interpreting the counter-office per-hour gain

The Discussion says that in counter offices "each hour worked was somewhat more productive". In queue-driven work there is a simpler explanation:
- With fewer staff present and unchanged demand, queues are longer.
- Staff therefore spend less time idle between contacts.
- Contacts per staff-hour rise mechanically because utilisation is higher, not because staff work more effectively.

The rise in waiting times and abandoned calls is exactly what this explanation predicts. If it is right, the +6.7% is mostly a cost passed to the public, not a productivity gain. The paper should present this alternative explicitly. Contacts per *occupied* hour, or handling time per contact, would help distinguish the two.

Two related points about the output measure:

- **Repeat contacts are counted as output.** The repeat-contact rate rose 0.9 points (11.8% v 10.9%). If repeat contacts count as "contacts handled", output is inflated by failure demand. The true loss in service may be larger than 11.4%.
- **Abandoned calls are unmet demand.** The 11.4% fall is in contacts handled, not demand served. Someone who gives up and calls back later may be counted twice or not at all.

## 4. Possible spillovers between offices

Randomising at office level prevents contamination between colleagues. It doesn't prevent contamination through shared workloads:

- **Contact centres.** Telephone lines are often pooled across sites. If calls route to whichever agent is free, control agents absorb calls the treated offices couldn't take. That inflates control output and exaggerates the treated–control gap.
- **Counter offices.** The public may switch to a nearby control office when queues lengthen.
- **Case-processing.** If cases can be reassigned across offices in the county system, the same issue arises.

The paper should state whether queues and caseloads were office-specific. If they weren't, it should show control offices' incoming volumes before and after.

## 5. Hours measurement and cost

**Unclaimed overtime is not counted.** Timesheets "include any overtime claimed". Unclaimed overtime is missed, and that is most likely among case-processing staff clearing backlogs. Missed hours would make actual hours too low, so the per-hour gain would be overstated.

**Cost is absent.** Case-processing staff worked about 3 hours a week of overtime on top of a full salary for 30 scheduled hours. Depending on overtime rates, labour cost per case may have risen even though output per FTE was roughly flat. A table of wage bill plus overtime per unit of output, by stratum, would turn "little or no loss of output" into a policy-relevant result.

**Restoring coverage has a price.** For counter offices, restoring coverage at 30 hours each would need roughly 25% more staff-hours. The trial held headcount fixed, so it answers "what if nothing else changes", which the Discussion should say plainly.

## 6. The meetings analysis

The caveats are appropriate, and registering a confirmatory test is the right move. A few additions would help.

**The correlation is very uncertain.** r = 0.71 across 7 offices has a 95% CI of roughly −0.1 to 0.95, so it isn't distinguishable from zero.

**There is no pre-period.** Calendar data exist only for month six. The 3.3-hour gap is a post-treatment comparison of 7 v 7 offices, and with so few offices, baseline imbalance is possible.

**A rough decomposition supports the authors' hypothesis.** This assumes treated and control offices started at about 7.1 meeting hours:

| | Control | Treated |
|---|---|---|
| Actual hours | 37.9 | 33.0 |
| Recurring meetings | 7.1 | 3.8 |
| Hours outside recurring meetings | 30.8 | 29.2 |

Non-meeting time fell only about 5%. Output per non-meeting hour then rose roughly 3% (0.979 / 0.948). If confirmed, most of the 12.5% would come from removing meeting time rather than from more productive working time. This could be reported as an illustrative calculation, with its assumptions stated.

**The policy question is what happens if meetings are cut without cutting hours.** The current design can't answer it. A meetings-only arm in the follow-up would be the most informative addition.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Define FTE.** "Output per FTE" should state whether a treated employee on 30 hours counts as 1.0 or 0.8 FTE. The results imply headcount-based FTE, but the text should say so.
- **Appeal outcomes lag.** Decisions made in months 7–9 will mostly not have been appealed and resolved by the nine-month analysis, so the case-processing quality measure is incomplete. Revisit it at follow-up.
- **Time-to-decision is missing.** Backlog size or time to decision against statutory deadlines would directly address the concern in the Limitations section.
- **Control resignations may be affected by the trial.** The 7.4% control rate may be inflated if control staff were demoralised by not being selected. A pre-period comparison would help.
- **Clarify the Summary.** Say that output per FTE in case-processing was held partly through overtime. Mention the rise in repeat contacts alongside waiting times.

## Relation to the Halden pilot

These results bear out several of the concerns raised about the Halden paper:
- Per-hour gains measured against scheduled hours roughly doubled here (12.5% → 22%).
- Actual hours fell much less than scheduled hours.
- Coverage-bound work behaved differently from backlog work.

Halden's retail and hospitality output fell 6.9%, compared with 11.4% here in counter offices. That is directionally consistent, since Halden's manager-reported index would be expected to look rosier.

## Overall

This is a credible trial with appropriately modest conclusions. The core finding is solid as far as it goes: backlog work absorbed a cut in hours with little loss of output per employee, while presence-bound work did not. The changes most worth making are:
1. small-cluster inference;
2. DiD estimates with CIs for wait times, quality, sick days and resignations;
3. a statement on whether queues were pooled across offices;
4. reframing the counter per-hour gain as plausibly a utilisation effect; and
5. a cost-per-output analysis.
